hook: Kurt Godel was born on April 28, 1906, in Brno, then part of Austria-Hungary and now in the Czech Republic, and enrolled at the University of Vienna in 1923 to study mathematics after beginning in physics. In 1931 he published his incompleteness theorems, proving that any consistent formal system powerful enough to describe basic arithmetic contains true statements that cannot be proved within that system, and that such a system cannot prove its own consistency. The result answered a central question posed by David Hilbert's program to place all of mathematics on a complete and provable logical foundation, and it did so by showing that goal was unreachable. Godel first visited the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton in 1933 and, after the Nazi annexation of Austria closed off his position at the University of Vienna, emigrated permanently to the United States in 1940. He became a full professor at the Institute for Advanced Study in 1953, worked there for the rest of his life alongside Albert Einstein and John von Neumann, and died on January 14, 1978, in Princeton, New Jersey.
name: Kurt Godel

quote.text: It is reasonable therefore to make the conjecture that these axioms and rules of inference are also sufficient to decide all mathematical questions which can be formally expressed in the given systems. In what follows it will be shown that this is not the case.
quote.context: From his 1931 paper On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems I.

quick_facts: Born April 28, 1906, in Brno, then Austria-Hungary and now the Czech Republic, and died January 14, 1978, in Princeton, New Jersey.
Studied mathematics at the University of Vienna starting in 1923.
Published his incompleteness theorems in 1931 at age 25.
First visited the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton in 1933 and emigrated to the United States permanently in 1940.
Became a full professor at the Institute for Advanced Study in 1953.
His incompleteness results are cited as an early formal boundary on what any computational or logical system can prove about itself.

achievements.title: First and second incompleteness theorems (1931)
achievements.impact: Proved formal limits on what any consistent axiomatic system can prove, a result that underlies later work in computability theory and the theoretical limits of machine reasoning.

achievements.title: Constructible universe in set theory
achievements.impact: Showed the consistency of the axiom of choice and the generalized continuum hypothesis with the other axioms of set theory, advancing foundational mathematics used across logic and computer science.

achievements.title: Decades at the Institute for Advanced Study
achievements.impact: Worked alongside Einstein and von Neumann for more than two decades, shaping mid-twentieth-century mathematical logic from one of its most influential centers.
